items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: The tree already cites S3, Pennsylvania Death Certificates, for Patrick's death on 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County, but records no parents or birthplace from it. Re-read the certificate image in 'Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968' (name-searchable) for the parents' names and birthplace, and the informant. It is derivative evidence on parentage. The tree gives Ireland ~1845 for birth, while the question says Pennsylvania; the certificate may settle which.

Patrick's own burial entry, as a baptism may not exist: the birth is either in Ireland or in Pennsylvania ~1845, and the birth parish is unknown. Burial entries often give age and origin. Search 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' (name-searchable). Catholic registers sit with the Archdiocese of Philadelphia, not the county (loc_001), so also check the cemetery record.

Requested by the researcher. 1870 US Federal Census on Ancestry (name-searchable index, paid) fills the gap between the 1860 census (cited in the tree as S2) and the 1880 census. Patrick would be about 25: look for him in Thomas Flynn's household or in his own, and for neighbors. Try variant spellings (Flinn, Flin, Flyn, Patt, Patk). The 1870 census does not give relationship to head, so household membership alone does not prove parentage. Verify against the image.

Baptism of Patrick ~1845, only if it exists: the 1850 census (log_001) places him at age 5 in Thomas Flynn's household, dwelling 84, Schuylkill, but the tree gives birth in Ireland. Search the name-searchable Schuylkill church records collection for baptisms naming Thomas and a mother, with variant spellings. A baptism would place the child with the parents.

Dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818, Ireland; tree) to the candidate mother. It would confirm the couple as a unit, supply the mother's maiden name only if it was her first marriage, and its date relative to ~1845 would corroborate parentage. It does not by itself prove Patrick is their child. The marriage may be in Ireland, so also check Philadelphia-area registers. Pair with the 1880 and probate items to test whether the mother's surname is her own.

The 1880 census records relationship to head and the birthplaces of each person's parents. If Patrick lives with Thomas, or lists parents' birthplaces, that tests the 1850 household link across 1860 and 1870. Also check for the mother as a widow.

Thomas Flynn's will or administration at the county Register of Wills (1811 onward, loc_001). Thomas was born ~1818, so he could die anywhere from 1850 to about 1900, and the window is sized to his lifespan rather than Patrick's. 'Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994' is browse-only (personCount 0), so browse the Schuylkill images. Heirs named would be direct evidence. Also check for any estate of the mother.

FAN and sibling records. Baptisms, marriages and burials of other Flynn children in Thomas's household (dwelling 84, 1850) and of adjoining households. They would name the same parents and sponsors, and sponsors are often kin, which tests whether Thomas is Patrick's father. Patrick's own marriage record and his children's baptisms (sponsors, grandparent names) also belong here.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

| # | ID | Type | Focus | Repository |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | pli_006 | Church | Patrick's children's baptisms (sponsors) and his marriage witnesses | FamilySearch — Schuylkill Co. sacramental registers |

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

Feliciana Parish split into East and West Feliciana Parish in 1824. items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

FAN item on brother Patrick Sheahan: tree F4/S1 records that in 1875 Patrick purchased land from James Kelly (Deed Book 42, p. 118), so a brother was in Schuylkill seven years earlier, a possible pull factor besides mining. Check the deed for Patrick's occupation and witnesses, and search deeds/leases for Michael as grantee or witness. loc_001 notes laborers often leased from mining companies, so absence of a Michael purchase is not negative evidence.

The 1900 census (name-searchable; 1890 largely lost) gives occupation, year of immigration, years married and children's birthplaces, which show where the family lived before the move and whether mining continued.

Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950 (name-searchable) for Michael's marriage and for Patrick's: gives residence, occupation, birthplace and parents' names. Pre-1906 deaths have no civil registration (loc_001), so also check Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968 (name-searchable) for Michael's death, occupation (cause such as miner's asthma or accident) and birthplace.

Local anthracite-region newspapers (Pottsville and nearby, to locate via repository catalogs) for 1880s colliery openings, labor demand, strikes, and mentions of Michael or Patrick Sheahan, including mine accident notices and obituaries. items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

Search Patrick's 1880 census household and neighbors: if Michael lived with or beside him, the move followed a sibling (family chain migration) rather than, or in addition to, mine work. Patrick's deed is a purchase by a brother, not Michael's own land record.

Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable. loc_001: Catholic registers stay under the Philadelphia diocese and are held at parish level. Search Michael, Patrick and the Sheahan surname (variants Sheehan, Shehan, Shean, Sheahen) for baptisms of children, marriages, and sponsors/witnesses, which show when the family arrived, which parish and mining town, and kin or associates. Does not by itself give the cause of the move.

Michael's own marriage, if after 1882, is in Pennsylvania, County Marriages 1885-1950 (name-searchable, 1921317) or Civil Marriages 1677-1950 (1571957). Marriage entries state residence, occupation and sometimes birthplace and parents, bearing on where he came from and whether mining was his trade at marriage. loc_001: no statewide civil registration before 1906, so earlier events fall to church and probate.

Michael's own death certificate (Pennsylvania Death Certificates 1906-1968, name-searchable, 2255255317 not cited; collection 2255317) gives birthplace, parents' names, years in the state and occupation (miner or other), the usual route to origin when no baptism is in hand. Window set by Michael's likely life span after 1906; if he died before 1906, rely on church burial (item 3) and cemetery records.

Context for the family tradition, not proof of Michael's own motive. Third-party or Pennsylvania newspaper archive; no collection URL was returned.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.notes: 1870 census: Michael Sheahan, farmer, household outside Schuylkill County. Establishes the 'before' point -- not yet in the coal region and not yet employed in mining.

1882 city/county directory: Michael Sheahan, occupation 'miner', Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. Establishes the 'after' point. Neither record explains the move itself -- found incidentally, not part of any plan.

items.question: Did Michael Sheahan move to Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania around 1882 for anthracite coal-mining work, as family tradition holds?
items.rationale: log_001 places Michael as a farmer in a different county in 1870; log_002 places him in Schuylkill County by 1882 with occupation 'miner'. The occupation and location both changed between these two points, consistent with a work-driven relocation to the anthracite coal region, but nothing yet directly documents the move itself or its cause -- no land purchase, employment record, or correspondence has been found. No plan has yet been written for this question.

entry.rationale: Tree fact F2 records Residence 1882 Schuylkill County and F3 Occupation 'Miner' 1882; log_001 shows a farmer outside Schuylkill in 1870. The 1880 census (name-searchable, collection 1417683) tests whether he was already in the coal region before 1882 (undermining a move 'around 1882') and shows household, birthplace, mining-related occupation, and neighbors (FAN) who may be co-workers or kin from the same origin.

Later censuses (name-searchable, 1900 and 1910 collections) show whether the miner occupation persisted, the years of immigration or residence, and children's birthplaces, which can date the move and reveal intermediate residences between 1870 and 1882. The 1900 schedule also gives months married and relationship to head.

loc_001 says Catholic sacramental registers stay with the parish/Archdiocese of Philadelphia, not the county. The name-searchable church collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH (Schuylkill County) may hold baptisms of his children, marriages or burials naming residence or earlier parish; sponsors are FAN. Dated to when he and his family lived there, as an early-arrival marker.

Coal-region local newspapers report new collieries, hiring, strikes, mine accidents and arrivals; a mention of Michael or of an operation hiring in 1882 would directly speak to the mining motive. Repository to be identified at search time (state/online newspaper archives, third-party sites).

Employment evidence: colliery payrolls, company records, Pennsylvania mine inspectors' reports, and mine accident or death reports naming miners. These are the primary records of mining work itself. Availability is unknown; locate through archive finding aids and the FamilySearch catalog (volume_search at search time).

Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683-1994 (collection 1999196) is browse-only (personCount 0), so this is an image browse of Schuylkill estate files. Pre-1906 deaths have no civil registration (loc_001), so a will or administration may name occupation, relatives and prior residence. Window runs to his plausible death, not just 1882.

Michael's own death entry: Pennsylvania Death Certificates 1906-1968 (collection 2255317, name-searchable) give occupation, birthplace, years in residence and parents, if he died after 1906. Before 1906, rely on church burial and probate items. May also state a mining-related cause of death (miner's asthma, accident).

Naturalization and church films for the coal region are browse-only (loc_001). If Michael was an immigrant, a naturalization declaration or petition states residence and arrival dates and can place him in Schuylkill before or after 1882. Browse image-by-image; volume_search at search time to locate the image groups.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Tree fact F2 records Patrick's death 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County, sourced to a Pennsylvania death certificate (S3), but the project holds no extraction of what it says about parents. Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968 is name-searchable and statewide registration began 1906 (loc_001), so the 1908 certificate should name father, mother (with her maiden name) and birthplace, and its informant. Derivative information, so a lead to be tested. Also serves as the subject's own death entry, since the tree gives his birth as Ireland (F1) while the question says PA, so a baptism in Schuylkill may not exist.

The only census searched is 1850 (log_001-003), which has Patrick age 5 in Thomas Flynn's household, dwelling 84 (indirect evidence only, ps_001). Timeline t_001 flags 1851-1860 as a gap with the 1860 census unsearched. United States Census 1860, 1870 and 1880 are name-searchable. 1880 records relationship to head and parents' birthplaces, so it can test whether Thomas remained Patrick's father figure and whether a wife appears. Use variant spellings (Flinn, Flynne, Floyd/Flin).

entry.rationale: Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records is name-searchable. loc_001: Catholic registers stay at parish/diocese under Philadelphia, not Scranton, and there was no civil registration before 1906. Look for baptisms of Patrick's siblings, burial of Thomas and any wife, and Patrick's own marriage or burial entries, which may state parents or a home parish in Ireland. Tree gives birth place as Ireland (F1), so Patrick's own baptism may be in Ireland rather than here.

It does not alone prove Patrick is their child. Likely in Ireland or an early Pennsylvania church register, so search the church collection and Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 (name-searchable) as leads only. County marriages begin 1885, too late for this marriage.

Patrick's own marriage record (and records of his marriages if more than one) typically names parents. Pennsylvania, County Marriages 1885-1950 and Civil Marriages 1677-1950 are name-searchable. Window set by Patrick's adult life, from about age 20 to his 1908 death.

A will or administration naming Patrick as son or heir would be direct evidence, and heirs lists name siblings.

FAN item: siblings, and neighbors in the 1850 household vicinity (dwelling 84, family 91), who may be kin. A sibling's death certificate, marriage or baptism naming the same parents, or an in-law, or godparents or witnesses in the church registers, would show whom Patrick's parents were. Sibling death certificates after 1906 are name-searchable and name both parents.

Tree records Patrick and Thomas as born in Ireland (F1, F3), contradicting the question's PA birthplace. Naturalization papers and passenger lists for Thomas (arrival before 1850) or Patrick may state the origin county and date of arrival. loc_001: coal-region naturalization films are browse-only, so browse images by volume.

Burial entries and obituaries (Find a Grave, local newspapers, cemetery registers) for Patrick (d. 1908-03-12), Thomas and possible relatives often name survivors, birthplace and parents, and place family plots together, which reveals siblings.

---

### What the tree already records

- Her 1879 marriage to James M Neal in Hill County, Texas, styles her "Landham" — apparently a widow's name at that point.
- A Smith County marriage of "M J Wood" to W F Lanham on 7 Jan 1869 is the earliest marriage record found; a bride born ~1859 would have been about 10, so that record may not be her, and "Wood" may not be her birth surname.

---

| # | Plan Item | Collection / Repository | Rationale |
|---|-----------|------------------------|-----------|
| pli_001 | Census 1860, **Blount County, Alabama**, FamilySearch | Name search for "M M Wood" household | Early lead — not yet linked to Martha; tests a possible birth family |

| pli_004 | **Marriage records, Hill County, 1879–1890**, FamilySearch | Covers 1879 Neal and 1888 Hamby marriages, including witnesses/bondsmen | Witnesses may be kin |
| pli_005 | **Death & burial records, Texas, 1888–1938**, FamilySearch; also Jimmie's 1938 New Mexico death certificate | Martha's own death/burial entry; Jimmie's death certificate may name maternal grandparents | Texas death certificates begin 1903 |
| pli_006 | **Probate, Hill County, 1853–1935**, FamilySearch | Full-text keyword search for a parent's estate naming Martha as heir | Estate papers often name daughters by married name |
| pli_007 | **Blount County, Alabama marriage records + neighbors of the Wood household, 1840–1880**, FamilySearch | Family, associates, and neighbors item | Corroborates or refutes the Alabama lead |
| pli_008 | **Church & cemetery records, Georgia and Alabama, 1855–1870** | Fallback for pli_001; needs a Georgia locality survey first | — |

Execute **pli_001** and **pli_002** (census searches) first, then work through the marriage records. A Georgia locality survey should run before pli_008.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

## Vélez-Málaga, Málaga, Spain — 1835-1870

Before civil registration (1871) the parish books are the vital record. Santa María's books from 1837 are on FamilySearch, unindexed but full-text searchable; one births volume for 1841-1845 is name-indexed.

items.question: Who were the parents of María Josefa García Romero (born about 1843, Vélez-Málaga, Málaga, Spain)?
items.rationale: Primary research objective. She carries two surnames and no parent is in the tree; nothing has been searched yet.

entry.jurisdiction: Santa María parish, Vélez-Málaga, Málaga, Andalusia, Spain
entry.rationale: The tree holds only a birth of about 1843 in Vélez-Málaga and no parent. loc_001 says civil registration began in 1871, so the baptism is the primary record, and entries normally name both parents and four grandparents. The 1841-1845 births volume (004458370) is name-indexed in part, so search María Josefa García Romero there first (variants Josepha, Joséfa, Garzía; also García alone), within the name-searchable Spain Baptisms and Catholic Church Records collections too. Subject is not a project-tree ark person, so no hints review.

entry.jurisdiction: Santa María parish, Vélez-Málaga, Málaga, Andalusia, Spain
entry.rationale: Fallback to item 1 if the index misses her (the volume is only partly name-indexed). Santa María registers from 1837 (image group 004104131) are not name-indexed but are full-text searchable: run an unscoped full-text co-occurrence of García and Romero as separate terms with María Josefa, via search-full-text, and browse the 1841-1845 images. Per Spain Naming Customs, she carries father's surname first then mother's, so García would be the father's and Romero the mother's, but scribes can reverse them; treat as unsettled until a record names the parents.

Dedicated item for the candidate parents' marriage to each other (a García and a Romero) in the years before her birth. It confirms them as a couple, gives the mother's birth surname (women keep their maiden surname in Spain per the naming-customs page) and, by date relative to about 1843, corroborates parentage. It does not alone prove she is their child; a baptism or household record must place her with them. Search Santa María and any other Vélez-Málaga parish registers; extend range earlier in case of an older sibling-era marriage or a second marriage.

FAN item: baptisms of possible siblings naming the same García and Romero parents, with godparents and grandparents, plus godparent records for María Josefa. Reveals the couple's household and the grandparents' names, and tests whether a candidate couple fits when her own baptism is ambiguous (common names García and Romero). Mode: create. Question q_001: "Who were the other children born to Bridget Halloran and her first husband, John Doyle, beyond the one already identified (Ellen Doyle)?"

I wrote the plan but have not run any of its searches. I have no search tools in this role, so executing it is a hand-off. That hand-off is search-records for the FamilySearch items (pli_001 to pli_007 and pli_010). The newspaper and cemetery items (pli_008, pli_009) go to search-external-sites.

What the tree and log already record:
- Bridget Halloran (I1) was born about 1838 in Ireland. The tree has no source for this and no other facts for her.
- John Doyle (I2) and Ellen Doyle (I3) have no facts in the tree and no sources attached.
- The 1900 census (log_002) records Bridget as mother of 9 children with 2 living, so about 7 children are unidentified.
- A marriage record (log_001) shows Bridget, described as Doyle by first marriage and Halloran by maiden name, marrying Martin Kearney in 1879 in Schuylkill County. John Doyle therefore probably died or left before 1879.
- Ellen's own marriage (log_003) names her parents as John Doyle and Bridget Halloran, which is the source for John's given name.
- None of the 3 logged searches belonged to a plan.
- Nobody has a FamilySearch ark, so I added no hints-review item.

Plan pl_001, in execution order. All are FamilySearch unless noted.
1. pli_001, church, Schuylkill County, 1855-1880. Baptisms of Doyle children are the main source because civil birth registration did not start until 1906 (loc_001). The church collection is name-searchable.
2. pli_002, census, 1860-1880. These are name-searchable. They should show the Doyle household with its children, and the 1880 Kearney household with any stepchildren.
3. pli_003, census, 1900-1910. This looks for the second surviving child.
4. pli_004, marriage, 1855-1880. This is Bridget and John Doyle's own marriage, which fixes the child-bearing window.
5. pli_005, marriage, 1865-1920. This is a sibling route: marriage records naming John Doyle and Bridget Halloran as parents, as Ellen's did.
6. pli_006, death certificates, 1906-1968. These name parents and informants for Bridget, Martin and any surviving Doyle child.

8. pli_008, cemetery, other repository. Burials of infants and of John Doyle.
9. pli_009, newspaper, other repository. Obituaries and death notices listing survivors.

It ends with estate papers, burials and newspaper obituaries, with a fallback of browsing the church register images by hand.

Next, the FamilySearch searches will run in that order, starting with the baptism registers.

## Muhlenberg County, Kentucky — c. 1870-1890

Statewide death certificates begin 1911; no certificate can cover a death in the 1870s-1880s. County death registers (1804888) exist but the 1860s-1870s coverage is partial. items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

The Schuylkill County Church Records collection is name-searchable; search Bridget with variants Kerrigan/Kerrigen/Kerigan/Carrigan, Bridgit/Bridget/Brigid, with parents Thomas and Ellen (Burke/Bourke). Baptism usually followed birth within days or weeks, so the window is narrow.

Fallback if the name search fails: the church-record image group is browse-only (personCount 0, 0% record-searchable per loc_001 and volume_search), so browse page by page through 1871-1872 entries for Pottsville Catholic parishes, reading for Kerrigan spelling variants since transcription and indexing may have missed her.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Seven plan items cover the necessary record types: censuses for household composition, vital records for marriage, military records for enlistment residence, pension files for household details, land records for property and neighbors, and probate for post-death household information. All items are sequenced and rationales explain their purpose.

dimensions.name: Tool Arguments
dimensions.rationale: All five MCP tool calls passed with correct arguments. project_context_query, research_query (plans, questions, localities), tree_query, and research_append all matched expected patterns. The research_append call correctly structured seven plan items with proper fields (sequence, record_type, jurisdiction, date_range, repository, rationale, fallback_for, status). No fixture_not_found errors occurred. Arguments were semantically correct.

dimensions.name: Record type selection
dimensions.rationale: Each record type is justified by the specific information need. Census (pli_001, pli_002) for household members and residence; vital_record (pli_003) for marriage and wife identification; military (pli_004, pli_005) for enlistment residence and next-of-kin; land (pli_006) for property ownership and neighbors; probate (pli_007) for widow and heirs. Rationales name what each type provides: 'census names every member of the household', 'marriage would name a wife, supply a residence', 'pension files name witnesses who are neighbors or kin (FAN)'. Record types directly answer the question's information needs.

dimensions.name: Objective scope containment
dimensions.rationale: Every item's rationale ties it to evidence about Josiah Rowe himself, not relatives' records for their own sake. The marriage item (pli_003) explains it would 'name a wife, supply a residence and explain who shares his household'—what it reveals about Josiah. The pension item (pli_005) states it 'can state wartime and prewar residences, marriage date and place, and household members'—all about Josiah's residence and household. Land records (pli_006) 'place him in a township in specific years' and show neighbors. Probate (pli_007) names 'widow, children and heirs, indicating the household he kept.' No item pursues a relative's record for its own sake.

dimensions.name: Sequencing logic
dimensions.rationale: Sequence follows defensible logic: free/indexed sources first (censuses pli_001-002, pension pli_005), then county records (vital pli_003, military pli_004, land pli_006, probate pli_007). Narrow before broad: 1850 and 1860 censuses establish baseline, then military records anchor 1862 enlistment, then land records fill gaps between censuses, then probate after death. The pension item (pli_005) correctly reaches past the 1850-1865 window to 1934, with rationale explaining 'a pension or widow's application filed after his 1879 death can state wartime and prewar residences.' No item depends on evidence only a later item can supply. Date ranges are appropriate: censuses at 1850 and 1860, military 1861-1865, pension 1861-1934 (collection-sized), land 1850-1865, probate 1879-1890.

dimensions.name: Jurisdiction accuracy
dimensions.rationale: Jurisdictions are historically accurate for the 1850-1865 period. Vigo County, Indiana existed from 1818-present (confirmed by locality guide). The plan correctly names Vigo County for land, probate, and marriage records. Census items appropriately start with Ohio (birthplace) and Vigo (death location), reflecting the unknown 1850 residence. Indiana statehood (1816) predates the entire research window. No anachronistic jurisdictions or boundary changes are missed. The locality guide confirms Vigo County's existence and jurisdiction for the period.
